q: "The best beloved of all things in My sight is Justice"
t1: If you want to know how those authorized interpreters explained it, that is a separate question, and I can search for it.
reply:
The line you're pointing to comes from the Arabic Hidden Words, and the passage is the one I'd start with.

["The best beloved of all things in My sight is Justice; turn not away therefrom if thou desirest Me, and neglect it not that I may confide in thee."](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_106&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-bl5u.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-bl5u.394) — [*Fountain of Wisdom: Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20781), Bahá'u'lláh

The same sentence also appears in the Parallel Hidden Words in English, and the Bahá'í World, Volume VIII, numbers it as the second of the Arabic Hidden Words (see the [Parallel Hidden Words](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_hidden-words_arabic_1903) edition and the [Bahá'í World, Volume VIII](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/national-spiritual_the-bahai-world-a-biennial-international-record-volume-viii-95-and-96-of#p5212) entry). John Huddleston's [*The Search for a Just Society*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/books/john-huddleston_the-search-for-a-just-society) cites it in the same way, as Arabic no. 2.

The passage is worth reading whole, because it does more than praise justice. It says justice is a way of seeing: "By its aid thou shalt see with thine own eyes and not through the eyes of others, and shalt know of thine own knowledge and not through the knowledge of thy neighbor." ([Fountain of Wisdom : Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_106&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-bl5u.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-bl5u.394)) On that reading, justice is tied to independent judgment, and the line closes with "Verily justice is My gift to thee and the sign of My loving-kindness."

The passage gives its own sense, and it does not carry a commentary from 'Abdu'l-Bahá or Shoghi Effendi that I found in this search. q: "ye are the fruits of one tree and the leaves of one branch"
t1: What I notice is the logic of the image itself: a shared root and trunk means the variety among people is not separation but kinship, which is why the teaching moves straight from the image to love and harmony.
reply:
The fullest form of the saying is in the [*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780), where Bahá'u'lláh writes: ["Ye are the fruits of one tree, and the leaves of one branch. Deal ye one with another with the utmost love and harmony, with friendliness and fellowship."](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_27&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl3h.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl3h.351) — *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*. The image is that of one tree: humanity's many peoples are fruits and leaves of a single growth, and the sentence that follows turns that picture into a command about how to treat one another.

The same words appear earlier in the [*Tablet to Mánikchí Sáhib*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-to-manikchi-sahib-lawh-i-manikchi), which the library's introduction describes as the first place Bahá'u'lláh gives this anthem its now-famous form. The introduction is a modern commentary, so it tells us about the tablet's place in the corpus rather than adding to its teaching: it suggests a date around 1869–1872 in the early Akka period, and notes that the tablet is written in pure Persian. Its text is at [the Mánikchí tablet](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_lawh_manikchi_neshati).

Two other passages show the saying's reach. Fred Mortensen's recollections of 'Abdu'l-Bahá, in Justin Penoyer's account, cite it under the heading of the oneness of humanity, and a 1946–1950 volume of [*The Bahá'í World*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/national-spiritual_the-bahai-world-a-biennial-international-record-volume-viii-95-and-96-of) also quotes it as a standalone line. These are a memoir and a compilation, so they show how the saying was received and passed on rather than adding authority of their own.

What I notice is the logic of the image itself: a shared root and trunk means the variety among people is not separation but kinship, which is why the teaching moves straight from the image to love and harmony.

q: "Be generous in prosperity, and thankful in adversity"
t1: For the wording itself, the Epistle is the primary text; the other entries reproduce it.
reply:
The line you're asking about comes from the [*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780) by Bahá'u'lláh, where it opens a long list of qualities the reader is urged to embody. The full sentence reads: ["Be generous in prosperity, and thankful in adversity."](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_156&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl72.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl72.1546) — *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*. The same wording appears in the compilation [*Bahá'í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings), and in the Arabic-derived collection [*Ocean of Lights*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=447025), where the saying is cited as the opening of a prayer-like passage on steadfastness and trust.

It is worth noticing that the sentence is a pair. Generosity is paired with prosperity, and thankfulness with adversity, so the instruction is not only about how to act when things go well or badly but about keeping the same posture of giving and gratitude across both. The passage then moves straight on to neighbourly trust, care for the poor, and fairness in speech, which I read as showing that inner attitudes are meant to become outward conduct.

A second source, [*Pioneering Over Four Epochs*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=22148), is a personal journal rather than scripture. Its author quotes the aphorism while describing a hard day of marital conflict and admits how difficult it is to live out. I cite it only as an illustration of how the saying is felt by one believer, not as a teaching about it.

For the wording itself, the Epistle is the primary text; the other entries reproduce it.

> ["Possess a pure, kindly and radiant heart, that thine may be a sovereignty ancient, imperishable and everlasting."](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_11&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_32.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_32.130) — *The Hidden Words of Bahá'u'lláh*

This is the scriptural text itself, so it carries the highest authority of the three passages you may be weighing. Because that page is an automatically generated file, I would treat its wording as a convenience copy and rely on the first passage for the exact text.

If you are studying the opening, the heart of the counsel is the pairing of purity and kindliness with a radiant (or, in some renderings, luminous) heart, and the promise that this yields a sovereignty that is ancient, imperishable and everlasting. q: "Veiled in My immemorial being and in the ancient eternity of My essence"
t1: And Julio Savi's *A Nest on the Highest Branch* and Robert Weinberg's biography of Ethel Jenner Rosenberg both quote the Hidden Word, but as quotations within their own reflections, so they illustrate its use rather than explain its meaning.
reply:
The phrase is the opening of the Hidden Word on the Son of Man, and the passage it comes from is the best place to start. In the Arabic-derived English rendering, Bahá'u'lláh writes: ["Veiled in My immemorial being and in the ancient eternity of My essence, I knew My love for thee; therefore I created thee"](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_17&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_38.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_38.164) — [*The Hidden Words of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20809). The words you have in mind are the first clause, so the discovery is that the veiling is joined directly to love: it is because God is hidden in His own essence that the love is what it is, and creation follows from that love.

A second passage uses nearly the same wording in a very different setting. In the [*Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653), Bahá'u'lláh describes God as one who "is and hath ever been veiled in the ancient eternity of His Essence, and will remain in His Reality everlastingly hidden from the sight of men" — [the Book of Certitude, in the paragraph on God's unknowability](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_116&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_60.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_60.870). Here the veil is an argument about the limits of knowing; in the Hidden Word it is the ground of a relationship. Reading them side by side shows that the same theme of divine concealment is held as both a boundary and an intimacy.

Two further sources are worth knowing. Balyuzi's biography [*Bahá'u'lláh: The King of Glory*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21731) places the Hidden Words in the Baghdad years, when Bahá'u'lláh was walking by the Tigris and reflecting on God's nearness and man's remoteness, and he calls them "those never-changing, eternal verities" at the core of every revealed religion. And Julio Savi's [*A Nest on the Highest Branch*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/julio-savi_a-nest-on-the-highest-branch-reflections-on-human-success-prosperity-and-happiness) and Robert Weinberg's biography of Ethel Jenner Rosenberg both quote the Hidden Word, but as quotations within their own reflections, so they illustrate its use rather than explain its meaning.

The phrase "Man is the supreme Talisman" ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_od.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_od.1321)) comes from Bahá'u'lláh's [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783), the opening sentence of a passage on education: ["Man is the supreme Talisman. Lack of a proper education hath, however, deprived him of that which he doth inherently possess."](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_od.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_od.1321) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*

The sentence sets up the rest of the passage. A talisman is an object believed to hold protective or transformative power. Bahá'u'lláh says the human being carries that power inherently, and that its realization depends on education. The same passage continues: "Regard man as a mine rich in gems of inestimable value. q: "Let not a man glory in that he loveth his country"
t1: The comparison with the Persian proverb and with Yogananda's book is my own observation about how the same idea travels, not a doctrinal claim by either tradition.
reply:
The saying you're asking about appears in several places, and the closest match is in Bahá'u'lláh's own words. In the Star of the West, Bahá'u'lláh writes: ["Let not a man glory in this that he loves his country; let him rather glory in this that he loves his kind."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/us-bahai-news_star-of-the-west-7#p708) — [*Star of the West*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/news/mary-hanford-ford_star-of-the-west-selected-content-from-volumes-viii-x). The wording is nearly identical to the Persian proverb that Paramahansa Yogananda quotes in [*Autobiography of a Yogi*](https://siftersearch.com/library/hindu/modern/paramahansa_autobiography-of-a-yogi) (the quotation is attributed there to a Persian proverb, not to a scripture of his own tradition), so the sentiment crosses traditions.

A second passage gives the same teaching with a wider sweep. In the [*Fountain of Wisdom*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20781), Bahá'u'lláh says: ["It is not for him to pride himself who loveth his own country, but rather for him who loveth the whole world."](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_462&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blfy.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blfy.354) — [*Fountain of Wisdom: Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20781).

Shoghi Effendi places the saying within the wider teaching on unity, quoting Bahá'u'lláh in [*The World Order of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20894): ["The world is but one country and mankind its citizens."](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_109&selectionString=shoghi_effendi_world_order_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_en_5n.0~shoghi_effendi_world_order_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_en_5n.295) — *The World Order of Bahá'u'lláh*. Here the words are Bahá'u'lláh's, reported by Shoghi Effendi.

A note on the layers: the teaching itself is revealed Scripture (Bahá'u'lláh's words). Shoghi Effendi's use of it is authorized interpretation. The comparison with the Persian proverb and with Yogananda's book is my own observation about how the same idea travels, not a doctrinal claim by either tradition.

q: "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want"
t1: The passages here do not settle whether any Bahá'í authority has commented on this verse specifically, so I cannot say how the Writings or the Guardian treat it.
reply:
The line appears in several places in the passages, and the most interesting one for a Bahá'í reader is the pilgrim's note from Madrid.

The clearest version is the opening of Psalm 23 itself, which the Tanakh (JPS 1917) gives as ["A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-psalms/?paraId=para_325&selectionString=ketuvim_jps_1917_hallel_psalms_en-blc0.0~ketuvim_jps_1917_hallel_psalms_en-blc0.48) — [*The Tanakh (JPS 1917), Tehillim (Psalms)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21243). The King James text is the same in substance, and the Bahá'í library's Bible text carries the same verse.

The passage that answers your question most directly is in the pilgrim's account of Bahíyyih (Margaret) Ford's time in Haifa. She writes that by the third day, "there was only one thing that went around in my mind and that was: 'The Lord is my Shepherd, I shall not want — etc.'" — [a pilgrim's reflection](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/bahiyyih-margaret_s-pilgrimage-reflections-shared-in-madrid#p45) recorded in her [*Pilgrimage Reflections Shared in Madrid*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/bahiyyih-margaret_s-pilgrimage-reflections-shared-in-madrid). This is her own recollection of her inner state, not a teaching of the Guardian, so it illustrates how the verse was received rather than explaining its meaning.

A third usage is in Rashi's commentary on I Chronicles, which cites the verse in a different setting: David's reply to the instruction that he "shall shepherd" God's people. Rashi reads it as David saying that the work does not depend on him, since the Lord is his shepherd, and so he too will not be wanting in what he is asked to do. That is Rashi's reading, from the Judaica Press translation, and it is a Jewish commentary, not a Bahá'í or Christian one.

The passages here do not settle whether any Bahá'í authority has commented on this verse specifically, so I cannot say how the Writings or the Guardian treat it.

The phrase opens the Sermon on the Mount, and the sources I found show it in three settings. In the Douay-Rheims text it reads: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (["Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven"](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/8300) — [*Douay-Rheims Bible*](https://siftersearch.com/library/christian/bible-and-translations/various_douay-rheims-bible)). Aquinas, in the [*Summa Theologica*](https://siftersearch.com/library/christian/church-fathers/st-thomas-aquinas_summa-theologica-part-i-prima-pars), cites Augustine's commentary on the Sermon to link the phrase with the humble and the fear of the Lord (["the fear of the Lord is befitting the humble of whom it is said: Blessed are the poor in spirit"](https://oceanlibrary.com/summa-theologica_saint-thomas-aquinas) — *Summa Theologica*, quoting Augustine).

From the Bahá'í side, Ethel Rosenberg's notes on St. John's Gospel, recording 'Abdu'l-Bahá's explanations, take the phrase as a contrast between the disciples, who were poor and unlettered yet are still remembered, and the kings whose names have been forgotten (["how many kings and potentates of the earth have come and vanished"](https://bahai-library.com/rosenberg_notes_st_john) — [*Notes on St. John's Gospel as Explained by 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-j-rosenberg_notes-on-st-johns-gospel-as-explained-by-abdul-baha), Ethel J. Rosenberg, recording). This is a note of spoken remarks, so it reflects her recollection rather than a written text by 'Abdu'l-Bahá himself. The San Francisco talk transcribed by Aminu'llah Farid simply quotes the verse in its context.

The sources here do not settle how 'Abdu'l-Bahá read "poor in spirit" beyond the contrast Rosenberg records, so I would not build a fuller doctrinal claim on them.

q: "Blessed is the spot, and the house, and the place, and the city"
t1: The Bahá'í Song Book also sets the lines to music, which may be a pleasant way to meet them.
reply:
The line you're asking about is from a prayer revealed by Bahá'u'lláh, and the passage is a short, lovely catalogue of places: a spot, a house, a city, a heart, a cave, a sea, a meadow. What strikes me is the sweep of it. Sacredness is not confined to a temple or a holy mountain; it is named in the most ordinary and the most remote settings alike, wherever God is remembered and praised.

The fullest text is the prayer itself, in [Bahá'í Prayers](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-prayers/?paraId=para_3&selectionString=baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en_2u.0~baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en_2u.214), where it is printed as a single prayer under Bahá'u'lláh's name.

Two other passages quote the same line, and they are worth knowing because they show how the words were used:

- The Research Department of the Universal House of Justice, in [*Conservation of the Earth's Resources*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/research-department_conservation-of-the-earths-resources#p100), cites the line as an example of the "sanctity of nature" in the Writings, and presents it as Bahá'u'lláh's words. That is a research compilation, so its use of the prayer is a reading of it, not an interpretive ruling.
- In [*Sustainable Communities in an Integrating World*](https://bahai-library.com/7147), the same prayer is cited to make a point about place: almost any place can serve for worship, yet physical, community-based centers remain important for faith.

Put together, the passages suggest a tension worth sitting with. The prayer seems to affirm that any spot can become holy, while the community literature stresses the value of shared, built spaces. I read these as complementary rather than contradictory, though that reconciliation is my own reading and not something the sources state.

The Bahá'í Song Book also sets the lines to music, which may be a pleasant way to meet them.

q: "Religion is the greatest of all means for the establishment of order in the world"
t1: Whether that holds in practice is a question the texts leave for each reader to test.
reply:
The sentence you quoted comes from Bahá'u'lláh, and it appears in more than one place in this library.

The companion passage is in 'Abdu'l-Bahá's [Tablet to the Central Organization for a Durable Peace, The Hague](https://bahai-library.com/abdulbaha_lawh_hague_anonymous). It gives the reasoning behind the claim. That is the strongest textual basis for the idea that religion secures order from within, not only by restraint.

Two notes on how to read these together. The words of Bahá'u'lláh and of 'Abdu'l-Bahá are scripture and authorized interpretation. The 1985 message is guidance from the Universal House of Justice, which has legal authority for the community; it is not an interpretation of the texts. The Bahá'í World and the newspaper and statement pieces are secondary records that repeat the same sentence. Bic's [*Baha'i Statement on Nature*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=33610) uses it to argue for religion's role in ecological ethics. That is an application made by the authors, not a doctrinal claim.

My own reading, offered as such: the passage says religion gives order by changing the person, which is why 'Abdu'l-Bahá sets it against law. Whether that holds in practice is a question the texts leave for each reader to test.

q: "The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao"
t1: I would not want to present one of those readings as the established meaning.
reply:
The line you have in mind is the opening of chapter 1 of the [*Tao Te Ching*](https://siftersearch.com/library/tao/foundational-classics/laozi-tr-gia-fu_tao-te-ching-tr-gia-fu-feng-and-jane-english), and the passages translate it several ways. Two of the closest renderings are:

["The Tao that can be told of is not the eternal Tao"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu/?paraId=para_7&selectionString=tao_ocean_second_attempt_en_2z.0~tao_ocean_second_attempt_en_2z.110) — *Tao Te Ching*, tr. Wing-Tsit Chan

["The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu) — *Tao Te Ching*, tr. James Legge

Both say the same thing: whatever can be spoken, named or described is not the constant Tao. "Told of," "trodden" and "expressed in words" are different English choices for one Chinese word, *dao*, which can mean "way," "path" or "speech," and the translations differ on which sense they bring out. The passages do not settle which reading is best; that is a question for the Chinese text and its commentators, which none of these passages cover.

What the passages do not establish is how the line should be interpreted beyond its wording. Whether it is a claim about the limits of language, a warning against mistaking concepts for reality, or something else, the texts I can search do not say. I would not want to present one of those readings as the established meaning.

t1: ["Nothing short of His all-encompassing grace, His all-pervading mercy, could have possibly achieved it."](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_177&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_7o.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_7o.631) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*
reply:
Gleanings 27 opens with praise of the unity of God as the One who creates all things out of nothing. The passage is a meditation on creation rather than a teaching on practice, and it makes its point through a question: how could sheer nothingness, by itself, acquire the capacity to emerge into being? Bahá'u'lláh's answer is that only God's "all-encompassing grace" and "all-pervading mercy" could have accomplished this.

The key words to notice are "out of utter nothingness," "from naught," and "rescuing His creatures from the abasement of remoteness." ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_177&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_7o.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_7o.631)) Together they present creation as a movement from non-existence into existence, and salvation as a rescue from "ultimate extinction" into "His kingdom of incorruptible glory." The passage leaves the cause of creation with God and the grace that sustains it, without offering an explanation of the mechanism.

["Nothing short of His all-encompassing grace, His all-pervading mercy, could have possibly achieved it."](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_177&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_7o.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_7o.631) — [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783)

t1: The passage on its own gives the claim and the warning, and leaves the working out to the reader's own study.
reply:
Gleanings section CXXVII is a short passage in which Bahá'u'lláh addresses people who want to know God. His answer is that recognition of God comes through looking upon Him, not through studying the Cause from the outside or by one's own unaided meditation. Bahá'u'lláh's words are: "look, then, upon Me with Mine own eyes, and not with the eyes of anyone besides Me" (["look, then, upon Me with Mine own eyes, and not with the eyes of anyone besides Me"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_813&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_pb.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_pb.472) — [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783)).

The passage warns that without this, people will never be capable of recognizing Him, however long they ponder His Cause or meditate on created things. It ends by saying the Revelation has been manifested so that people may be roused from heedlessness and become "of them that understand."

Two points for a reader to weigh. First, the passage stresses that the eyes through which one should see are Bahá'u'lláh's own, which is a claim about the centrality of His station and not only a call to devotion. Second, the text itself does not spell out how recognition works in practice; for that, a reader would want to turn to the surrounding Gleanings sections and to the writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá. The passage on its own gives the claim and the warning, and leaves the working out to the reader's own study.

reply:
The Seven Valleys opens with the first valley, the Valley of Search (Valley of Seeking), and this passage is the one most readers meet first. Bahá'u'lláh describes the seeker's journey from the dust of this world to the divine homeland as seven stages, noting that some writers name seven valleys and others seven cities, and then says the seeker must first leave self behind before entering the sea of nearness and union. The first valley is the valley of seeking, and its steed is patience. He warns that a traveller without patience will never reach the goal, and that the seeker must never grow disheartened, even after a hundred thousand years without seeing the Beloved's beauty.

The passage asks for more than endurance. Then the seeker sees all existence searching for the Friend, with Jacobs wandering in search of Joseph and a whole world running after the Beloved. The passage closes by measuring this longing against the madness of Majnún, the lover who was found throwing dust and weeping, which the text leaves at its most striking point.

Where the text stops is worth noticing. It describes the ardour of the seeker in vivid, almost lyrical terms, but it does not spell out the practices a reader should take up. For that, the seeker turns to the later valleys and to the guidance of the Writings as a whole, and each reader will find their own way into what patience and purification mean in daily life.

Read the full text here: [The Seven Valleys](https://oceanoflights.org/bahaullah-pub06-068-fa/#:~:text=%D9%88%20%D8%A8%D8%B9%D8%AF%20%D9%85%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%AA%D8%A8%20%D8%B3%D9%8A%D8%B1,%D9%86%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%8A%D8%AF%20%D8%A8%D8%A7%20%D9%87%D8%B1%20%D8%AC%D9%85%D8%B9%DB%8C) — [*The Seven Valleys*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-seven-valleys_fa)

reply:
[*Paris Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20908) (also published as *The Wisdom of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*) is a collection of addresses delivered by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá during His stay in Paris in 1911, capturing notes taken by listeners during His public talks and private interviews.

**Scripture:** Revealed scripture comprises the writings of the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá; because *Paris Talks* consists of pilgrim and listener notes taken down during ‘Abdu’l-Bahá's addresses rather than authenticated Tablets in His own hand or dictation, it does not carry the rank of revealed Scripture.

**Authorized Interpretation:** The Guardian, Shoghi Effendi, approved the use and distribution of these records, as seen when publications and compilations reference works such as [*Paris Talks*](https://oceanlibrary.com/women_bahaullah/?paraId=para_89&selectionString=women_compilation_ocean_en-bl57.0~women_compilation_ocean_en-bl57.18) [*Women*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/research-department-compilations/research-department_women), but the Guardian's own writings and authorized translations stand as the definitive standard for interpretation.

reply:
[*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780) is Bahá’u’lláh’s final major work, addressed to Shaykh Muḥammad-i-Taqíy-i-Najafí—known as the Son of the Wolf—who was a prominent and hostile cleric in Iṣfahán.

**Scripture**
The text itself stands as revealed Scripture, written by Bahá’u’lláh toward the end of His ministry to gather testimonies from His earlier writings, warn His persecutors, and set forth the fundamental principles of His Revelation.

**Authorized Interpretation**
Authorized commentaries and tablets by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá frequently reference or cite the [*Epistle*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780) to elucidate its historical context and spiritual significance, noting its unique position as a summative address to the religious leadership of Persia.

**Universal House of Justice Guidance**
The Universal House of Justice and its Research Department draw upon passages from the *Epistle* as source material within thematic compilations guiding administrative matters, social action, and community life.

**History and Scholarship**
Historical studies and introductory expositions, such as those by John E. Esslemont in [*Bahá’u’lláh and the New Era*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20813) and David S. Ruhe in [*Robe of Light*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-s-ruhe_robe-of-light-the-persian-years-of-the-supreme-prophet-bahaullah-1817-1853), treat the *Epistle* as a vital historical document that captures Bahá’u’lláh's final appeals for justice and understanding directly to the clerics who opposed Him.

t1: [Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_607&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.966) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*
reply:
Gleanings 100 is Bahá'u'lláh's call to those who would teach His Cause: keep your garment free of worldly stain, and go out with hearts detached from created things and reliance upon God. In the passage's own words, "It behooveth them to choose as the best provision for their journey reliance upon God, and to clothe themselves with the love of their Lord." ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_607&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.966)) The promise that follows is that such teachers' words "shall influence their hearers," so the power of teaching is tied to the inner condition of the teacher rather than to eloquence or technique.

The passage also gives a picture of the inner life it asks for: minds "wholly centered" on God, hearts "completely detached from and independent of all things," ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_607&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.966)) and souls "sanctified from the world and its vanities." Detachment here is not a rejection of the world, since the passage asks the teacher to "spread it abroad on the earth," but an orientation in which one's loyalties are not divided.

This is my reading of the passage; the text itself does not spell out how such detachment is practised day to day, so for that you would want to turn to the wider Writings or to the authorized interpreters.

[Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_607&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_jl.966) — [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783)

reply:
The Dhammapada opens with the teaching that our present condition is shaped by our thoughts: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." It then gives the consequence of an evil thought in a simile, that "pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage" ([*The Dhammapada*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20925), Siddhartha Buddha, [read here](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha/?paraId=para_4&selectionString=the-dhammapada_en_2t.0~the-dhammapada_en_2t.195)).

The passage's own words settle the main point: thought comes first, and speech and action follow from it. The passage does not go beyond this, and I haven't found anything in these sources on how the teaching is read elsewhere in the tradition.
